io_floor: 4K fixture (907.2 MB) on the NVMe SSD: plain File.Copy takes 0.24-0.34 s from a warm source and 0.42-0.51 s from a cold one (Windows caches the write). An unbuffered write-through copy takes 0.86-1.88 s. A sequential read takes 0.38 s cold (2.37 GB/s) and 0.22-0.24 s warm. A raw 'ffmpeg -i in -map 0 -c copy out.mp4' of the whole file takes 0.86-1.47 s (warm and cold about the same), and demux only (-f null) takes 0.84-1.25 s. 1080 fixture (228.6 MB): File.Copy 0.05-0.09 s, ffmpeg -c copy 0.22-0.28 s. The ffmpeg step of SplitEngine's 3-part 4K split takes 0.74-0.78 s, so split export runs at the ffmpeg -c copy floor (verified). On the box's SATA HDDs (about 150-190 MB/s, from the drive specs, not measured) a cold read of the same file would take roughly 5-6 s (inferred).

ranked_hotspots: 1. Bulk Cut 'Exact' precision (SmartCutEngine head re-encode). 4K: 6.45-7.17 s per file at intro 10.5 s; x3 = 21.4 s, run sequentially (BulkTrimEngine.cs:188). 1080: 3.0 s per file (under load). The head alone takes 4.3-5.5 s at intro 10.5 (1080: 1.26), 22.8 s at intro 104.5 (1080: 5.13), and 130.7 s at intro 540.5 of a 10-min 4K file. The cost grows with intro position because SmartCutArgsBuilder.cs:113-119 uses OUTPUT -ss, which decodes from the file start (89% of the file read at 104.5). Input seek gives identical frames in 4.4-5.3 s at any position. With veryfast/NVENC: 1.4-2.2 s. HEVC 4K: 20 s at intro 44.5 vs 6.8 s input seek, and the HEVC output is corrupt after the joint (separate correctness bug).

2. Join run (JoinEngine.JoinAsync, 3 parts): 4K 2.8-4.5 s vs 1080 0.9-1.2 s; three parts of the 10-min file 8.1-9.4 s (under load). 1.4-2.2 s of it is 6 sequential, uncached ProbeAsync calls (CheckCompatibility at JoinEngine.cs:86 plus SumDurations at :246, 0.27-0.30 s each on 4K H.264 vs 0.10 at 1080). The concat itself takes 1.4-2.3 s vs 0.86-1.47 s for a one-file copy of the same bytes. Adding clips costs 1.6-2.9 s for 3 clips (6 more probes) vs 0.46-0.68 at 1080, and every remove or reorder re-probes all clips.

3. Hover / scrub thumbnails (Split timeline hover, Bulk chips and profile): 0.50-0.63 s per grab plus a 60 ms debounce at 4K vs 0.17-0.21 s at 1080 (3x). A 10-position sweep takes 5.45 s vs 1.86 s. On 4K with a 10 s GOP, a mid-GOP grab takes 1.74-2.03 s. About 0.25 s of every 4K H.264 grab is find_stream_info (-nofind_stream_info: 0.25/0.38 s, identical picture).

4. Bulk add rows (3 x 4K): runnable after the keyframe scans at 1.93 s (cold 2.51), chips drawn at 2.87 s (cold 3.41). 1080 under load: 0.99 / 1.45 s. Bulk Lossless run: x1 1.20-1.25 s, x3 4.32 s vs 1080 0.70-0.83 / 2.55 (under load).

5. Split LOAD until Split is enabled (the keyframe scan, which reads 100% of the file): 4K 0.95-1.05 s (cold 1.33) vs 1080 0.30-0.32 (cold 0.42). On the 10-min 4.5 GB file: 4.8-5.4 s (1.73 for the 2-min file under the same load). The preview can open after the probe: 0.27 s (1080: 0.10). Waveform 0.64-0.70 s runs in parallel. Inferred: on the box's 5400-rpm HDDs a cold 4.5 GB file needs about 24-30 s of read before Split is enabled. A moov-index keyframe read gives the identical list in 0.003-0.006 s from 0.1 MB.

6. Split export (3 lossless parts): 4K 1.08-1.64 s vs 1080 0.33-0.35; 10-min 4K 5.1-6.0 s (under load). The ffmpeg step takes 0.74-0.78 s, the same as a raw whole-file ffmpeg -c copy (0.86-1.47 s) on the same disk. The only extra is the re-probe at SplitEngine.cs:121 (0.27-0.35 s). VERDICT: split export is AT the IO floor. On this machine and these fixtures the slow feel is not the export. It comes from the 4K costs around it: the full-file keyframe read at load (and the HDD, if the user's files live there), the 3x slower thumbnails and preview, the ~0.25 s H.264 find_stream_info tax on every ffmpeg/ffprobe call, the probe repeated 6-12 times per join, and above all the Bulk Exact cut.
notes:
VERIFIED vs INFERRED. Everything with a number was measured with the harness. The harness drives the real Core services (MediaProbe, FfmpegThumbnailService, FfmpegWaveformService, SplitEngine, JoinEngine, BulkTrimEngine, SmartCutEngine builders) through the app's own FfmpegRunner/FfprobeRunner, in the call order the view models use (cited file:line). Only synthetic fixtures were used. No user files, no GUI, no %APPDATA%/%LOCALAPPDATA%. The repo's git status is clean (only normal Core bin/obj were built). INFERRED, not measured: HDD timings (rules kept me off the F:-J: HDDs; estimate = bytes read / ~150-190 MB/s). Not reproduced: FFME Player.Open and real preview scrubbing. ffmpeg decode throughput stands in for them. My fixtures are 1-10 min long. Real footage is often longer, so costs that grow with file size scale with it. Verified from 2 min to 10 min under the same load: keyframe scan 1.29 -> 2.9 s, LOAD 1.73 -> 5.0 s, split 1.68 -> 5.5 s, join 4.3 -> 8.6 s, Exact head at a late intro 30 s -> 131 s.

WHY 4K COSTS MORE (verified). (a) Every ffmpeg and ffprobe call on 4K H.264 pays about 0.24 s of single-threaded find_stream_info decode: probe 0.27 vs 0.035 with -nofind_stream_info, and HEVC 4K is only 0.035 to begin with. ProbeAsync has no cache (MediaProbe.cs:78-147). So the cost repeats: split prepare (SplitEngine.cs:121), each Join chip, compat and SumDurations (4 probes per clip over add plus run), Bulk row add plus the Exact engine re-probe (SmartCutEngine.cs:78, KeptMiddleRequestBuilder.cs:39). (b) The keyframe scan reads 100% of the file, every byte (GetProcessIoCounters), even though the cache keeps it once per file. (c) The Exact head uses output seek, so the decode grows with cut position. (d) Pixel-bound work (thumbnail decode, Exact encode) scales about 3-4x from 1080 to 4K, which is expected.

CORRECTNESS FINDINGS, found while checking equivalence; out of perf scope, all variants affected equally. 1) HEVC Exact output is corrupt after the head/tail joint in the current engine path. The concat output keeps the libx265 head's hev1 extradata, and the tail's slices (whose parameter sets live only in the source hvc1 extradata, per trace_headers) decode with 250-316 errors ('alignment_bit_equal_to_one=0', 'Too many refs'), frame md5s that differ from the source, and tail PSNR 11-15 dB. Evidence file: t187-fixtures/work/smart2-final-current-hevc-10.5.mp4. H.264 survives because the concat/mov path inserts SPS+PPS in-band before the tail IDR (the decoded frames after the joint are md5-identical to the source). 2) In H.264 Exact outputs, TailCopy (-ss before -i, -c copy, -avoid_negative_ts make_zero) gives the tail a video start_time of 0.080 s against audio at 0.000. In the final, the first tail frame lands at 1.6 s instead of 1.5 s, and about 80 ms of audio overlaps at the joint (verified with frame md5s and ffprobe). 3) The comment at SmartCutArgsBuilder.cs:91-93 says the output seek 'decodes from the previous keyframe ... bounded by one GOP'. Measured: it decodes from the file start.

MEASUREMENT CONDITIONS. The night runs were quiet and repeatable. The 2026-10-04 runs were made while other sessions kept 6-15 of 20 logical cores busy, which inflated CPU-bound timings about 1.6x (the same-load 2-min re-run quantifies it). Within-run comparisons hold. Cross-run 4K-vs-1080 ratios for Bulk compare night 4K with loaded 1080, so they understate the 4K gap.
